extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in the history and philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A concise encyclopedia overview comparing major early-20th-century philosophies of mathematics (logicism, formalism, intuitionism, constructivism, Platonism, finitism) and key technical concepts (completeness, consistency, decidability, Gödel/Church results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logicism (mathematics reducible to logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logicism: mathematics is reducible to logic; if all logic were understood perfectly, then all mathematics could be derived from it or considered part of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated with Frege and taken in a weaker form by Russell and Whitehead; motivated the attempt to derive arithmetic and other mathematical theories from propositional logic and formal languages (e.g., Principia Mathematica).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peano axiomatization of arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Peano introduced five axioms for the arithmetic of the natural numbers (the 'Peano postulates'), which influenced investigation into the foundations of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an example of the move toward formal axiomatization of mathematics and the use of formal systems and well-formed formulas (wffs) to represent mathematical theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalism (aim to formalize mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalism attempts to reduce mathematical problems to formal statements and then prove that the resulting formal systems are complete and consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's formalism accepted some Platonist ideas but varied; part of the Hilbert program was to resolve paradoxes of infinity and to show formal systems' soundness by proving completeness and consistency of foundational systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical system is complete when every valid or true statement in that system is provable in that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness was a desideratum of formalist programs (i.e., that formal systems capture all truths expressible in the system). Gödel's incompleteness results bear directly on the attainability of this goal for sufficiently expressive systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is consistent if it contains no contradictions, that is, if some statement p does not imply both q and not-q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving consistency of foundational systems (e.g., propositional and predicate logic) was a central aim; several historical consistency proofs (Post, Ackermann, Hilbert, Gentzen) addressed parts of this program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platonism (mathematical realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platonism: mathematical objects exist as ideals, independent of worldly experience, and can be discovered by thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with constructivism and intuitionism; some versions of formalism accepted Platonist commitments while others were more syntactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivism (existence via construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructivism: mathematical objects exist only if they can be constructed; a mathematical proof is acceptable only if it arises from the data of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposes Platonism; often allied with intuitionism. For constructivists, existence claims require explicit constructions or algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitism (only finite demonstrations accepted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Finitism recognizes the existence of only those mathematical objects that can be demonstrated in a finite number of steps or proved in a finite number of wffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert and many followers were finitists; finitism is a more restrictive stance within the broader formalist program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitionism (mathematical objects as mental constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitionism claims that the only real mathematical objects are those that can be experienced (mentally conceived); mathematical proofs are assertions of the reality of mathematical objects, not just series of wffs, and proofs are necessary, not just sufficient, to assert reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuitionism often aligns with constructivism and rejects certain classical logical principles (notably the law of excluded middle). Brouwer emphasized mental construction (Kantian intuition of time) as the basis for mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the law of excluded middle (LEM) in intuitionism
rubrics_metrics.description: Intuitionism rejected the law of the excluded middle (as established by De Morgan) and questioned Cantor's concept of infinity because of its unintelligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection implies that some classically valid existence or disjunction arguments are not acceptable to intuitionists unless constructive evidence is provided; Heyting later formalized an intuitionistic propositional logic respecting this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert program (23 problems and programmatic aims)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the 1900 International Congress Hilbert presented 23 problems; the Hilbert program (with later modifications) became the agenda of formalism, aiming to resolve foundational issues (such as paradoxes of infinity) and to secure mathematics via formal proofs of consistency/completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program motivated much foundational work in the early 20th century; Gödel's incompleteness theorems later showed fundamental limitations relevant to the program's goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system or theory is decidable if there is a way (algorithm) to determine whether a given sentence is a theorem of that system or theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decidability results (e.g., Lukasiewicz and Post for propositional logic) were viewed as supporting formalist aims; undecidability results (Church/Turing) showed limits for certain logics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gödel incompleteness (limitation on formalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gödel's two incompleteness proofs (1931) showed inherent limitations of sufficiently expressive formal systems, dealing a telling blow to the ambitions of formalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gödel's results show there are true statements in such systems that are unprovable within the system, undermining the goal of complete formalization of all mathematical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undecidability / Church's theorem and Church–Turing distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Church (and independently Turing) proved in 1936 that first-order logic is undecidable (Church's theorem). This is distinct from the Church–Turing thesis, which concerns what functions are effectively computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undecidability shows there is no general algorithm to decide theoremhood for first-order logic, limiting mechanistic/algorithmic ambitions for complete decision procedures in logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitionistic formal systems (Heyting logic / self-sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heyting formulated a propositional logic in accordance with intuitionistic/constructivistic principles (1930); McKinsey showed Heyting's axioms for intuitionistic propositional logic are self-sufficient (1939).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formal systems provided a rigorous syntax/axiomatics for intuitionistic reasoning, showing that constructivist principles can be captured in formal logics distinct from classical logic.
